title: Prokaryotic cells and viruses; Cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation

Terms and clues: CE04b#t1 term and clue written for the game; CE06#t1 term and clue written for the game; CE04b#t3 term and clue written for the game; CE06#t3 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Capsid
items.clue: Coat of protein around the genetic material of a virus

items.label: Homogeniser
items.clue: A blender used to break open the cells of chopped tissue

items.label: Reverse transcriptase
items.clue: Enzyme carried by HIV; having it is what makes HIV a retrovirus

items.label: Supernatant
items.clue: The liquid above the pellet, poured into a fresh tube and spun faster

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell

questions.explanation: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.stem: Liver tissue is homogenised in an ice-cold, isotonic, buffered solution. Why must the solution be isotonic?

options.text: So the liver cells do not burst before the organelles can be collected.
So that enzymes released from the cells are denatured and cannot digest the organelles.
So that the pH of the homogenate stays constant while the organelles are being separated.
So organelles do not gain or lose water by osmosis, and do not burst or shrivel.

questions.explanation: With equal water potential inside and outside, there is no net movement of water, so the organelles keep their structure.

questions.stem: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?

options.text: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolises them to build copies of itself.
It must first acquire a DNA molecule, because one RNA strand cannot act as genetic material.

questions.stem: Which conclusion do the data support?

options.text: Most mitochondria are in pellet 2, but pellet 2 is not a pure sample of mitochondria.
Pellet 1 contains nuclei and nothing else.
Mitochondria are the densest organelles, as they are found in the first pellet.
Ribosomes are larger than mitochondria, as they need the fastest spin to be collected.

questions.explanation: Pellet 2 holds 84% of the mitochondrial enzyme, but also 5% of the DNA and 6% of the rRNA, so some nuclear material and ribosomes are mixed in.

questions.stem: Bacteriophage lambda does not multiply in a sterile nutrient broth containing amino acids, nucleotides and ATP, but does multiply when living E. coli cells are added to the broth. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The phage's own enzymes and ribosomes work only once they are activated inside a cell's cytoplasm.
The phage lacks ribosomes and most enzymes, so it needs a cell's protein synthesis machinery.
The phage cannot absorb dissolved nutrients from the broth, but it can feed on the contents of a cell.
The phage has to attach to a cell wall before it can grow large enough to divide in two.
